en: The Sūtra of the Youth Sudarśana, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Vaiśālī, at the Āmra Grove.

Within the Lāvaṇī Garden, he was together with the śrāvakas, eight thousand bhikṣus, ten thousand bodhisattvas, and this entire great assembly, all of whom had transformed their forms and garments to take on the bodies of devas.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl; surrounded by this assembly of transformed beings before and behind him, he entered the great city of Vaiśālī to beg for food in sequence, gradually proceeding until he arrived at the house of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti.
At that time, within the house of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, there was a young boy named Subhūṣita.

At that moment, Subhūṣita was on the upper story of his own mansion, held in the arms of his nurse. The boy was playing with and toying with a single lotus stalk held in his hand. Because he had been perfumed by the many roots of goodness planted in past lives, and through the supernatural power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the boy suddenly addressed his nurse in verse, saying:
"Now there is a sound most subtle, That eclipses all musical tones."
"I pray that you, Nurse, release my body and set me down upon the tower.
For this radiance shines; it must surely be a Great Man who, with his right foot treading the threshold, desires to enter this city gate."
Subtle and exquisite, causing the mind to rejoice, are the calls of these various birds;
such singing by the birds as this, my ears have never heard before.
Surely this is the Tamer of Men, acting for the benefit of the world.
With his right foot treading upon the threshold, he was about to enter this city gate.
Adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, his entire body emitted a resonant sound;
its tone was exquisite and melodic, bringing joy to all who heard it.
With feet marked by the thousand-spoked wheels, his body adorned with majestic power,
he placed his right foot upon the threshold, desiring to enter this city gate.
It was like a great earthquake, and also like the striking of a bronze bell.
All such sounds as these are heard by none who fail to hear them.
On that day, the light from the body of the Great Sage was most certain;
wishing to enter this great city, he brought fearlessness to all sentient beings.
Like the various trees in the forests, adorned with diverse flowers;
each hears a subtle and wondrous sound according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
Firmly and securely established is the Great Dragon King Who Grants Wishes.
With his right foot treading upon the threshold, he was about to enter this city gate.
Like the illumination of light from the void, the great earth was everywhere bright;
the radiance of the sun was eclipsed and no longer shone, for this was the golden hue of the World-Honored One.
Observing with resolute joy, emitting flames of great majesty,
he placed his right foot upon the threshold, intending to enter this city gate.
Now, Grandmother, behold these hosts of devas in the sky!
With sounds of joyful song and laughter, and playing with various garments and ornaments,
he who brings certain benefit to the world and is the most supreme among all beings stepped his right foot across the threshold, desiring to enter this city gate.
Now, within this great city, they face one another with hearts of loving-kindness;
each rejoices together with the others, as a parent loves a child.
They are certain to possess a great mass of merit, their bodies adorned with manifold virtues.
With his right foot treading upon the threshold, he was about to enter this city gate.
Furthermore, men and women brought various kinds of incense and flowers;
filling their cupped hands, they scattered them in all four directions, their hearts filled with great joy.
The Great Sovereign, resolute and adorned with the flowers of merit,
places his right foot upon the threshold, desiring to enter this city gate.
Flowers scattered by devas and humans completely fill the void of space.
Everywhere a rain of various fragrances falls, subtle and most delightful.
The Sugata, certain of the world, enters the city with great merit and wisdom;
for the benefit of sentient beings, he has now come here.

At that time, as the nursemaid held the boy in her arms, she heard these verses spoken from his own mouth; her heart was struck with terror, the hairs on her body stood on end, and her limbs trembled so violently that she could not support herself.
Having placed the boy upon the upper story of the pavilion, he immediately reflected thus:
"What kind of being is this child?
Is he a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a kumbhāṇḍa, a piśāca, a kiṃnara, or perhaps a mahoraga?"
"Such words as these are not spoken by an infant of the world.
At that time, the nursemaid immediately stood still and did not dare to move; she neither rose to walk nor dared to speak loudly, but breathed softly, lowered her head, and listened in silence.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually approached the house of the Licchavi youth Subhūti, entered the street, and stopped before his gate.
Then the Licchavi youth Sudarśana, seeing the World-Honored One from afar at the foot of the pavilion, immediately threw himself down from the high tower toward the Buddha.
At that time, the Licchavi youth Sudarśana, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, stood poised in mid-air and addressed the Buddha in verse:
“The World-Honored One dwells within wisdom; The Most Victorious One abides here.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I pray that you will accept these lotus flowers.”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Licchavi youth Subhūti with these verses:
“The ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in which I abide is not the realm of sentient beings;
That limit is non-existent; this limit is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).”
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the Licchavi youth again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
“How does the World-Honored One abide in this reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)?"
"If this limit does not exist, where can that which is non-existent abide?
At that time, after the Licchavi youth Subhūti had spoken these words, the Buddha further replied with a verse:
"That which is like the limit is the actual limit; that limit is the Tathāgata."
As that reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) abides, so do I abide therein.
As all Buddhas are identical in essence with the reality-limit,
and as that true reality-limit is such, I abide in this manner.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the youth Subhūti again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
“Neither limit nor non-limit—what are the characteristics of this limit?”
“By what kind of skillful means is it called the ‘true reality’ (bhūtakoṭi)?
When the Licchavi youth Subhūti had spoken these words, the Buddha further replied in verse:
“One cannot grasp at a limit as a limit; Therefore, it is called the ‘limit of reality.’”
“That limit is like space, and space, too, is without marks.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the youth Subhūti again addressed the Buddha in verse:
“How rare is this place of truth; it is the supreme dwelling among all dwellings!”
"May all sentient beings abide herein, just as the Buddhas abide.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the Licchavi youth Subhūti joined his palms with single-minded devotion and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will accept these lotus flowers."
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the Licchavi youth Sudarśana, accepted those lotuses.
Once the Buddha had accepted the flowers, the Licchavi youth Sudarśana leaped for joy and made this vow:

"By virtue of these roots of goodness, may I, in a future life, upon realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, preach the Dharma to all sentient beings just as the World-Honored One does now."
"However, within that Dharma, neither the dharmas of ordinary worldlings nor the Arhats, nor any of the dharmas of the noble ones can be apprehended.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra, being present in the assembly, having heard these words, addressed the Licchavi youth Subhūti in the midst of the great multitude, saying: "Licchavi youth!"
Regarding what you have just said— that after I have realized such a Dharma, I shall preach that Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings—
how does one preach the Dharma? What is that Dharma like?
At that time, the Licchavi youth Subhūti replied to Śāriputra in verse:
“In those dharmas there is no Buddha, nor are they attained by any śrāvakas;
I shall realize these dharmas and preach them for the sake of all sentient beings.”
That Dharma has no location, nor does it come or go;
the wise know it thus as the fundamental nature of phenomena.
All Buddhas of the past and the Unsurpassed Honored Ones of the present—
Knowing thus without exception, one enters the nirvana without remainder.
Within that state, there is no realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), nor is there a realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*);
such is the ultimate limit, wherein no one in the world enters.
“The Dharma-realm consists only of names; these names arise from conceptual discrimination.
Since discrimination is itself non-discriminative, ultimately nothing can be apprehended.
At that time, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, amidst the assembly, addressed the youth Sudarśana with a verse, saying:
"O youth, how is it that you are able to study and understand this Dharma?
It is profoundly deep and beyond analogy, confounding even the wise.
Though your body has not yet practiced it, you have already produced such eloquence."
To the foremost among the great śrāvakas of wisdom,
Your nature is like pure gold, Thoroughly skilled in all understanding;
You illuminate the streets of this city, Like the moon dwelling in the void of space.
At that time, the Licchavi youth Subhūti immediately replied to the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra with a verse, saying:
"O Venerable One, you now speak of 'arising,' yet this arising has no location.
Since all phenomena are without arising, what is this 'arising' that you speak of?"
Since all phenomena are without arising, what can be called their true essence?
This, I say, is their intrinsic nature: that all phenomena are non-existent.
Both phenomena and their intrinsic nature are equally unapprehendable.
Since these two are both unattainable, this is the Dharma taught by all Buddhas.
It is called the Supreme Wheel, turned for the first time in the Deer Park;
having clenched his fist within empty space, he causes many śrāvakas to awaken.
I utter only the sound of the Dharma, for sentient beings are largely deceived and deluded;
relying on skillful means and wisdom, I shall speak according to reality.
To speak of "birth" and "death" is the realm of ordinary worldlings.
This inverted view has not yet been exhausted by Pūrṇa.
Birth and death, self and other, are the conventional speech of worldly people;
within the Dharma that is beyond speech, one speaks provisionally by means of language.
At that time, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard these verses, rejoiced and praised them, and then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, Blessed One!
"How marvelous, Sugata! This Licchavi youth Subhūti possesses such profound wisdom that it is difficult to measure.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇa, saying:
"So it is, so it is! Pūraṇa, it is just as you have said.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavi youth Subhūti with these words:
“Good Thought, youth!
For whom do you now wish to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
At that time, the Licchavi youth Good Thought replied to the Buddha in verse:
“The Buddha, the most supreme World-Honored One, knowing [the answer], asks me intentionally:
‘For whom do you wish to don the armor?
Now you should declare it truly.’”
I am a person of nothingness, nor do I wear the armor of attachment;
within this most profound and supreme Dharma, there are no sentient beings to be transformed.
Sentient beings are not sentient beings; all things are utterly non-existent.
One who is not deluded in this regard is called the World-Honored One.
Such is the Dharma that gives rise to understanding; it abides eternally as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
It is neither one nor different; this is the most profound and supreme.
I shall cause the assembly to awaken; yet those sentient beings do not exist.
Since the essence of sentient beings is non-existent, how could there be wisdom therein?
Wisdom and sentient beings—by their very nature, they ultimately do not exist.
"If one can understand in this way, they are called a person of worldly wisdom.
At that time, the Licchavi youth Subhūti, having spoken these verses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One!"
"If, when I have come and personally realized such a Dharma, I shall speak it thus for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu Ānanda rose from his seat within the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous, Bhagavān! How marvelous, Sugata!
This Licchavi youth Subhūti is indeed able to thus proclaim these profound and subtle phrases of Dharma—phrases that are unstained by attachment and phrases that are free from dependence."
Within this profound Dharma, the world of gods and humans is terrified, deluded, and submerged.
World-Honored One,
within such a reality-nature that is so profoundly deep, who would not wish to practice?
"Only those who have previously encountered the causal conditions within the profound Dharma are able to give rise to faith.
At that time, Ānanda, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just like a mass of pure gold, Seen from afar, it appears magnificent and radiant;
This youth Sudatta stands amidst the great assembly like Mount Sumeru securely situated within the ocean;
thus he expounds the sublime Dharma, pervading this entire world.
"Neither existence nor non-existence," thus spoke the youth Subhūti;
"such is that *bhūtakoṭi*, and the *bhūtakoṭi* is also empty and void.
When you spoke these words just now, you felt no fear."
"Good Thinking, you are thus; how can I come to know it?
At that time, having heard these words, the Licchavi youth Good Thinking immediately replied to Ānanda in verse:
"I have already vowed to sacrifice my body, donning this armor of the unconditioned."
Seeking the Way because there is no other hope, one comes to know thus through much hearing.
Bewildered by the five desires, one falls into the fearsome hells;
now that I behold the Unsurpassed Honored One, why should I not rejoice?
The World-Honored One, in great compassion, Transforms and delivers all sentient beings;
My body has not fallen or been injured, And now I stand before the Buddha.
Both empty space and my own body— These two are entirely non-existent.
Since both the body and space do not exist, why should one fear their destruction?
The essence of the Buddha’s body and of space is truly indivisible;
one who possesses such a mind of patient endurance has no fear therein.
In true suchness (tathatā), both space and the great earth are entirely non-existent;
I now know this with certainty, and for this reason I have no fear.
Space pervades the great earth, yet ultimately it cannot be apprehended.
Because there is neither truth nor birth, there is no real cause for alarm or fear.
Just as space has no height and likewise no low place,
so too for one who knows the Dharma in this way, there is no falsehood to cause alarm.
At that time, after the Licchavi youth Subhūti had spoken these verses, the Buddha asked him:
"Subhūti, young man, are you not afraid?"
At that time, Susīma replied to the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I am truly without fear.”
The Buddha again asked the youth Subuddhi:
"Are you not afraid? Subuddhi replied:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I truly have no fear.
The Buddha asked again:
“Child Sudharma! Are you not afraid? Sudharma replied:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I am truly not afraid.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Suvicintita, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-thought-out Licchavi!
Truly excellent!”
"It is well that you are now able to be thus without fear, without alarm, and without dread.
On account of this matter, the Buddha spoke these verses for Sutasoma:
"Because of existence, fear arises; yet that existence cannot be found."
One who can stabilize this patience is close to bodhi.
To grasp at signs and speak of "sentient beings" is to ignore that such beings do not exist;
one who can thus penetrate this understanding abides in the True Vehicle.
In awakening, there is no one who attains it; neither attainment nor non-attainment can be grasped.
Free from this attainment and non-attainment, the fearful mind ceases to exist.
If one can understand thus, one dwells in neither existence nor non-existence.
"Good Thought, you should know: this path leads to enlightenment.
Then, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One further addressed Good Thought, saying:
"Young man Good Thought!"

Therefore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly and securely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should constantly contemplate the marks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the marks of a sentient being, a life-span, a nourisher, and a *pudgala*. These marks constitute the true, direct path to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good Thought, young man!
When I first resolved my mind upon practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, I constantly kept this path in mind. For this reason, by riding upon this path, I attained bodhi.
Yet, within this path, there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended; this is precisely what constitutes my unsurpassed bodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Though I speak of the mark of permanence, That permanence is not something existent.
Once one knows that there is no permanence, Then there is no contention."
Those who perceive the characteristic of pleasure find that even pleasure lacks reality;
this is a perverted view, for they conceptualize a *pudgala*.
If one knows the truth of all phenomena, one realizes that each lacks a place of accumulation.
They do not perceive signs, nor life, nor the person (pudgala).
The path is not enlightenment, and that which is not the path is likewise so.
I declare this intrinsic nature: all phenomena have no fixed location.
The fundamental nature and all phenomena—the wise do not discriminate between them;
Subhūti, you should know this!
This is the path leading to enlightenment.
If one clings to such a path, that Buddha is not the path of practice;
if one clings to signs, one does not understand all dharmas, nor can one mount the vehicle. Such a person is the object of the Buddhas' compassion.
No one is able to traverse this tranquil and profound state.
In all places there is no thing; that which is a thing cannot be a thing.
Since no thing exists, that bliss has no place to arise.
All pleasures and all pains—this path is like empty space;
One who can attain such awakening, that mind shall be liberated.
Though I speak of the mark of a self, this dharma does not exist either.
Since there is no "mine," there is likewise no wisdom.
Since there is no wisdom that knows, this is precisely the realm of wisdom.
The conceptualization of a life-span exists, yet its characteristics are ultimately empty.
There is no one who knows by means of words; those of small wisdom are immediately deluded.
The mark of a self and a life-span—by their very nature, these do not exist.
This nature and all phenomena are the domain of the ignorant.
They cannot approach the inconceivable Buddha-vehicle;
they do not hear the profound sūtras, nor do they read, recite, or uphold them.
This sūtra does not speak of [them], for it contains no marks of dharmas.
I have not attained any dharmas, nor is there even a locus for them;
when I sat at the site of enlightenment in the past, there was not a single wisdom to be realized.
Such is this wisdom of mine: awakening is unattainable.
Bodhi and the site of enlightenment—these two have no one who realizes them.
It is the common folk who make such distinctions; the Buddhas teach all dharmas as mere conventional names, for this is the profound realm of the Buddhas.
The profound and the Buddhas—these are the realm of Māra;
They do not hear this sutra spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
They do not know the flavor, the place where all dharmas bring benefit.
The Bodhisattva practices asceticism, yet his practice is devoid of knowing.
One speaks of "Buddha" and "bodhi," yet these two cannot be perceived;
having reflected thus, one falsely claims that the Buddhas have taught them.
They speak of the existence of various objects, and by relying upon them, they give rise to attachment;
since there is thus a locus of defiled attachment, they do not perceive me.
If there are sentient beings who have perfected profound wisdom, [they likewise do not perceive me].
They proclaim with a great voice that the Buddhas are inconceivable.
Therefore, you should reflect well!
If you wish to know the profound Dharma, apply yourself with diligent attention, and you shall immediately know the reality of the Dharma.
That dharma is truly unimpeded, and is therefore called "profound";
when it is spoken of in this way, it is called "unattainable.
Sentient beings have inverted views; this is not within their sphere of experience.
The true meaning cannot be sought through meditative concentration;
Samādhi is not samādhi, for it cannot be found within emptiness.
This is not the domain of wisdom, and the same applies to the absence of wisdom.
Although one may cause that limit to be awakened to, it is nonetheless not the domain of discursive knowledge;
this dharma arises from conditions, and thus one can enter its profound depth.
If there is delight in tranquility, then there is neither "this" nor "that."
If one’s mind can have faith and joy in the place where this sutra is correctly taught, such a person has not been near only a single Buddha; they have planted various roots of goodness in the past.
Only after being in the presence of many Buddhas can one be able to receive and uphold this.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One further addressed the Licchavi youth Subhūti, saying: "Subhūti youth!
For this reason, all great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should don such armor.
Amidst whatever places of terror and dread exist within the world, they should not give rise to thoughts of alarm, fear, dread, or terror therein.
"Having given rise to this mind, one thus dons the armor.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying, "O Great Sage, World-Honored One!"
"I believe this, even though it is a point that is not believed in by the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Subhūti:
"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound; they possess such characteristics, such auspicious signs, and such forms."
All those noble beings perceive that within the world there are no phenomena that can be ranked as superior or inferior.
Having seen that all phenomena are equal and devoid of superiority or inferiority, and having realized this, their minds are neither afraid, nor terrified, nor startled.
"Having known that all dharmas are severed, one is not startled;
having known that all dharmas are not severed, one is not terrified."
“Having known that all phenomena exist, one is not startled;
having known that no phenomena exist, one is not afraid.
Having known that all phenomena are gathered together, one is not startled.”
Having understood that all phenomena are dispersed in this way, one does not fear.
Having understood that all phenomena are combined in this way, one is not startled;
having understood that all phenomena are not combined in this way, one does not fear.
Having known that one does not loathe any phenomena, one is not startled;
having known that one does not loathe any phenomena, one is not afraid.
"Having known that one does not contemplate all phenomena, one is not startled;
having known that one does not contemplate all phenomena, one is not afraid."
"Having understood that all phenomena are conditioned, one is not startled;
having understood that all phenomena are unconditioned, one is not afraid."
"Having thus understood all phenomena that are within one's sphere of experience, one is not startled;
having thus understood all phenomena that are beyond one's sphere of experience, one is not afraid."
"Having known that all dharmas are joyful, one is not startled;
having known that all dharmas are not joyful, one is not afraid."
"Having thus understood all phenomena of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one is not startled;
having thus understood all phenomena that are not of the conventional truth, one is not afraid."
"Having known that all phenomena are quiescent, one is not startled;
having known that all phenomena are not quiescent, one is not afraid."
"Having understood that all phenomena are thus resolved, one is not startled;
having understood that all phenomena are thus not resolved, one is not afraid."
"Having thus understood all dharmas of upholding the precepts, one is not startled;
having thus understood all dharmas of violating the precepts, one is not afraid."
"Having clearly understood all phenomena as they are, one is not startled;
having clearly understood the absence of clear understanding regarding all phenomena as it is, one is not afraid."
"Having known that all dharmas have names, one is not startled;
having known that all dharmas are nameless, one is not afraid."
"Having known that all phenomena emerge, one is not startled;
having known that all phenomena do not emerge, one is not afraid.
Having known that all phenomena are fearful, one is not startled;"
"All phenomena are without fear"—having known this, one does not tremble.
"All phenomena arise"—having known this, one is not startled;
"all phenomena do not arise"—having known this, one does not tremble.
"Having known that all phenomena are subject to death, one is not startled;
having known that all phenomena are not subject to death, one is not afraid.
Having known that all phenomena are bodhi, one is not startled."
"All phenomena are not bodhi; having known this, one does not fear.
All phenomena are nirvāṇa; having known this, one is not startled.
All phenomena are not nirvāṇa; having known this, one does not fear."
"When one is able to preach the Dharma in this manner, this is called a bodhisattva who is not afraid, not startled, not terrified, and not frightened.
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning for the sake of Suvicintin, spoke these verses:
"All dharmas do not exist; Suchness is without delusion."
Because all phenomena do not exist, their characteristics are themselves quiescent.
All phenomena lack superiority or inferiority; this and that are both entirely absent.
Since all dharmas are non-existent, even reality itself is likewise non-existent.
All phenomena have degrees of excellence or inferiority, yet both this and that are each non-existent;
since all phenomena are entirely empty, there is no contention or strife.
Since all dharmas are non-existent, how could there be a nature in their original nature?
Since their nature does not exist, how could there be destruction?
Do any phenomena undergo cessation?
The wise do not harbor such thoughts.
There is only the provisional name "cessation," yet when one seeks the locus of cessation, it cannot be found.
If one wishes to cease all phenomena, they cannot be found even when sought with subtle discernment;
whether minute or numerous, all phenomena are utterly non-existent.
That all phenomena are non-existent—this too is but a verbal expression;
therein they are thus non-existent, yet they are merely manifested within [conventional] reality.
All dharmas are formless, yet they appear only within the realm of signs.
Existence and non-existence—both are merely conventional designations.
All phenomena possess conjunction, yet they are shown to be without conjunction;
because True Suchness (tathatā) is without conjunction, ultimately there is no entity whatsoever.
All phenomena lack combination; they neither arise nor cease.
Thus they cannot be apprehended, for each phenomenon is individually non-existent.
Since all phenomena are unapprehendable, they have no prior limit.
Since the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi) does not exist, it is therefore called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi).
All dharmas are joyful, yet that joy cannot be apprehended;
since no dharmas exist at all, they likewise cannot be described.
All phenomena are without joy, and those two are both absent;
within suchness there is no entity—this is the profound characteristic.
All phenomena are without aversion, and within suchness there is no self.
Because true suchness does not exist, there is no basis for aversion toward it;
because nirvāṇa cannot be praised, that dharma is unattainable.
Since all phenomena do not exist, it is therefore called nirvāṇa.
That all phenomena are without ignorance is manifested within True Suchness;
this is spoken of as a provisional designation, and for this reason it is called "thought.
That all phenomena are without thought means that these phenomena have no fixed location.
Therefore, there are no sentient beings; this is the essence of all phenomena.
All phenomena are like illusions, yet that illusion cannot be apprehended.
Because phenomena cannot be apprehended, one speaks of conditioned formations.
Since all phenomena are unconditioned, they are the essence of suchness;
as there is no location for any phenomena, they are said to be boundless.
Although one speaks of "realms," in truth, no realms exist.
That which is spoken of by ordinary beings is therefore called an "objective realm.
Since all objective realms are false and illusory, they are said to be "without objective realms";
to speak of the non-existence of objective realms is the true reality of objective realms.
Regarding the essence of all phenomena, they are beyond numbering;
since they do not exist, you should know them as tranquil stillness.
Do not speak of attainment where there is no attainment, yet manifest the appearance of a place of attainment.
In the state where there is neither attainment nor non-attainment, attainment is manifested through appearance.
In that state, there is no upholding of precepts, nor is there any breaking of them;
there is no practice and no morality—such is the characteristic of all phenomena.
All phenomena are entirely non-existent; therefore, they are called ignorance.
Because no phenomena exist, you should know this to be clarity.
As for the names of all phenomena, those names are in reality non-existent.
Since there is no name for any dharma, one should know that this is nirvāṇa.
When it is said that there is a name for "feeling," it is manifested by means of feeling;
since in this state there is no feeling, it is therefore called the manifestation of feeling.
That which is non-existent appears as having the mark of existence; it is manifested and thus called "existent.

Sudhi, you should know: such is the Dharma I teach.

Good Thought, youth!

Good Thought, youth!

"Good Thought, young man!

Good Thought, youth!

"Good Thought, youth!

Good Thought, youth!"

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning for the sake of Sucintita, spoke these verses:

There is no place to be attained; this practice is the most supreme.
Where I practice this way, others act with perversion;

Startlement and the absence of fear— All phenomena are mere designations.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, the Licchavi youth Subhūti immediately realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having already attained that realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he became free from all worldly sorrow and joy and attained great bliss;
he then soared further upward into the void, rising to a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately smiled.

Now, it is the nature of all World-Honored Ones that when they smile, various rays of light issue forth from their faces; these lights are of many colors, namely blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, pale green, emerald, deep azure, and crystal. These radiances thus illuminate immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds, reaching even as far as the Great Brahma Palace at the Peak of Existence.
Having shone upon them, the lights return to the presence of the Buddha, circle him three times, and then enter through the crown of his head.

At the moment of his entry, this great earth shook with six types of eighteen modes: it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it subsided, subsided everywhere, and subsided equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere.

At that time, from the void of the higher realms, the heavens rained down various fine powders of *candana* sandalwood, aloeswood, powdered incense, and celestial flowers; and various kinds of subtle and wondrous celestial sounds spontaneously arose.

This trichiliocosm is pure and adorned, just like the northern continent of Uttarakuru; its magnificence and splendor are of one kind, without distinction, and this trichiliocosm is likewise without difference.

At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I do not yet understand for what cause and condition the Tathāgata smiles and emits this light;

The heavens of empty space rained down flowers as an offering to the World-Honored One;

Within the three thousandfold world system, all manner of adornments were purified.

“The light emitted by the World-Honored One, its rays of manifold colors, issued from the Blessed One’s face; please explain this cause for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Ānanda in verse, saying these words:

“Ānanda! From this day forth, this Licchavi youth Suvicintita shall make offerings to and revere billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of Tathāgatas, serving them without ever contravening their teachings.”

Furthermore, he made offerings to those World-Honored Ones, providing them fully with the four requisites of clothing, medicine, dwellings, and bedding. After those Tathāgatas had entered parinirvāṇa, he made offerings to their relics, constructing stūpas out of various jewels. Each of these stūpas was a hundred thousand yojanas in height, and within all those jewel stūpas he enshrined the relics, making offerings to those stūpas with various famous incenses.

Furthermore, they took all manner of flower garlands for adornment, all kinds of jewels, all kinds of banners, various exquisite flowers, and powdered sandalwood and aloeswood, and scattered them upon it.
Furthermore, he made offerings with various most exquisite sounds.

Having made offerings to those many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, he cast off his final body and attained Buddhahood, appearing in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Viśuddhacandra (Pure Moon)—the Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and World-Honored One.

“If one were to fill the worlds of the ten directions With all manner of rare and wondrous jewels,

“Having heard this Dharma-characteristic as proclaimed by the Great Sage,

Excellent, Great Holy One!

Like the dragon of Anavatapta, who pours down rain from the midst of space;

Those fourfold assemblies remain far removed from my Dharma practice;

Among all supreme dharmas, it is the very eye of the world.

for one who can uphold this sutra, there is no darkness whatsoever.

having understood this, one should not be indolent, but should read and recite this sutra.

This is the Dharma of all Buddhas, taught for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
having heard this sutra, they realize it is profoundly deep and inconceivable.
When this sutra was being spoken, all the Buddhas of the ten directions smiled and emitted rays of light, each declaring, "Excellent is this teaching!
You have raised up the great banner of victory, the inconceivable banner of the Dharma."
This four-line verse of the sutra, he expounds for the great assembly.
Skillfully employing many expedient means within the inconceivable Dharma,
those who can uphold this sutra further explain it to others.
That person shall converse with the Buddha and realize the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Honored One;
one who is able to uphold this sutra shall receive inconceivable empowerment.
At that time, having spoken these verses in response to Śāriputra, the World-Honored One further addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:

“Ānanda! If there should be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas or upāsikās, who in a future age are able to listen to this sūtra with faith, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, those persons shall obtain the greatest merit.”
That mass of merit is immeasurable and boundless; it is like the realm of space, such that no person can measure or know its limits. Even so, even so!
Venerable Ānanda!

If within this Dharma-text there is one who can receive and uphold even a single four-line verse—whether reciting it themselves or explaining it to others—the roots of merit and goodness that such a person attains are immeasurable, ineffable, and without limit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning for Ānanda and the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"If one can read and recite this, The body of boundless skillful means, It will benefit many sentient beings; The King of Consecration acts out of compassion."
Even if I were to speak for now, the void might be measured;
yet if one wishes to compare it with this sutra, it can never be fully exhausted.
All Buddhas of the ten directions, the supreme Honored Ones in the world;
If one upholds this sutra, one has made offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions,
those Kings of Dharma who have severed birth and death;
the person who can uphold this sutra is said to have already made offerings to them.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, Those who sever the roots of the ten evils,
And those who hear this sutra— Such people can make offerings to all those sages. I,
as well as the Buddhas of the future And the Tathāgatas of the past, [rely upon them].
To all those currently in the ten directions, The Unsurpassed Honored Ones among two-legged beings,
Who can let out the lion’s roar— To them all, one should make offerings;
One should be able to receive and uphold this sutra, As proclaimed by all the Buddhas.
One who makes offerings with material wealth is not a person of true wisdom;
if one can uphold this sutra, they are the foremost among all offerings.
Even if one were to fill the worlds of the ten directions with the seven treasures and practice generosity;
The merit of one who maintains this sutra even slightly surpasses that of making offerings to all the World-Honored Ones.
To study this scripture is to be like a consecrated king;
this reverence for all Tathāgatas is manifested within true suchness.
Regarding all dharmas that I have taught, not even the Buddhas can be apprehended therein;
those who hear this and are not struck with fear or terror are truly making offerings to the World-Honored One.
This offering is profoundly deep, such that none in the world understand it.
Neither grasping nor rejecting—this is the most supreme offering.
Regarding all Buddhas and all dharmas, one neither grasps nor rejects;
this is the most supreme offering, praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
In the past, when Dīpaṃkara Buddha was present, I made offerings to this Dharma;
this offering is the most supreme, as taught for all bodhisattvas.
At that time, in the presence of that Buddha, I maintained these offerings.
That Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction: "You shall become a Buddha.
If you wish to become a Buddha and furthermore be the foremost among sentient beings, you should accomplish this path; this is called making offerings to the Buddha.
Through making such offerings as these, I have now attained the Way of the Buddha;
having thoroughly penetrated all dharmas, I am worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans.
All the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones who are supreme in the world;
Riding upon this most supreme offering, the foremost among all offerings,
you shall realize the Buddha-realm and inconceivable wisdom;
you will be able to let out the lion’s roar, fearless just as I am now.
Having uttered the lion’s roar, he attained mastery over all dharmas;
he liberated the multitudes of sentient beings and entered untainted nirvāṇa.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the youth Sudarśana, the entire great assembly of Vaiśālī, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, and non-humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, all believed and accepted it, and joyfully put it into practice.
The Scripture of the Youth Sudarśana, Scroll II.
